tier_reason: docs/performance.md compares opuspp against the reference libopus 1.6.1 decoder (opus_decode_float) on the same packets (same 320 kb/s bitrate, encoder complexity, 10 ms frame size, fullband stereo, 48 kHz float output); the harness opuspp/tests/bench.cpp and the build/run driver opuspp/tools/profile_report.py are public, and the page states compilers (GCC 16.2, Clang 22.1), identical flags per profile for both decoders, and the CPU (Ryzen 5 9600X, one pinned core). Every number in claimed_speedup matches the tables in docs/performance.md and docs/performance-additional.md.

corrections.caveats: Code was written by Claude Code (the README says so); the repository has one commit (2026-10-02), 0 stars and no users yet. Decoder only, and only for one stream configuration: OPUS_APPLICATION_RESTRICTED_CELT, fullband, 10 ms frames, 48 kHz stereo float output, prediction disabled, encoder complexity 0-4, no SILK/hybrid/FEC/pitch post-filter; other packets are rejected. The comparison is like for like: both decoders decode the identical packet buffer, built with identical flags per profile (libopus with its default CMake options apart from hardening off, so its intrinsics/run-time CPU dispatch stay enabled), best of 7 passes with the packet buffer clflushed before each pass. Output is bit-identical to libopus in the Size (-Os) and Balanced (-O2) builds (47 encoder configurations and a 300k-packet fuzz test per docs/verification.md); the Fast builds (-ffast-math, FLOAT_APPROX) are not bit-exact in either decoder (about 137 dB SNR on normal frames and 62 dB in concealment against libopus FLOAT_APPROX), so the fastest-build comparison is perceptually, not bit-exactly, equivalent. Only rendered tables are committed; the raw results.json that profile_report.py writes is not in the repository, and the numbers were not re-run. libopus is linked statically; docs/performance-shared-library.md reports 1.24x to 1.48x against a shared libopus. The GCC -Os opuspp build is 0.88x of the fastest libopus build (GCC Fast).

notes: Checked the orchestrator's points: harness, compilers, flags and CPU are all public; comparison is against reference libopus 1.6.1 at the same bitrate, complexity and frame size on the same packets; bit-exact only in the strict-IEEE (Size, Balanced) profiles, not in Fast. Metadata (BSD-3-Clause derivative of libopus, 0 stars, 1 commit on 2026-10-02, not a fork) confirmed on the GitHub page.

tier_reason: Upgraded C to B: the numbers are an independent measurement (Keukhan of OvenMediaEngine, no VideoLAN affiliation; PR #2336 merged) against libaom 3.12.0's decoder with the CPU model, RAM, OS, governor, decoder versions, thread counts and clips stated. Not A: no benchmark script or command is public, compiler and flags are unstated, and the clips are not published; dav1d's own repo (README, NEWS) carries no numbers against libaom.

corrections.claimed_speedup: OvenMediaEngine PR #2336 (libaom 3.12.0 vs dav1d 1.5.4, max decode rate, 4K60 AV1): game clip 22.3 vs 74.7 fps at 4 threads (3.3x) and 26.0 vs 74.1 fps at 6 threads (2.9x); camera clip 20.2 vs 61.1 fps at 4 threads (3.0x) and 22.1 vs 67.6 fps at 6 threads (3.1x). The PR summarises 'about 3x faster at the same thread count'. Snippet only (blog/medium pages not opened): single-threaded 1.5-2.5x and multi-threaded 2.3-4.5x faster than libaom.
corrections.caveats: The numbers come from a third-party pull request description, not a benchmark suite: no script or exact command is linked, compiler flags and assembly settings are unstated, and the 'game' and 'camera' clips are not public. dav1d 1.5.4 was built with meson and used through FFmpeg (--enable-libdav1d) with max_frame_delay=2, a low-latency setting that limits frame threading; libaom's build options are not stated. Same thread counts (4 and 6) for both decoders. One old machine (2x Xeon Silver 4114, Skylake-SP). dav1d's README and NEWS carry no numbers against libaom; its checkasm --bench only compares its assembly against its own C code. The 1.5-2.5x / 2.3-4.5x figures are snippet only. Canonical repository is code.videolan.org/videolan/dav1d; the GitHub repo is a read-only mirror.

corrections.caveats: Snippet only: all numbers come from search-result snippets of blocked papers (SiPS 2015 'Parallelization of Kvazaar HEVC Intra Encoder for Multi-core Processors', 'AVX2-optimized Kvazaar HEVC intra encoder', 'Kvazaar HEVC encoder for efficient intra coding', and 'Performance evaluation of all intra Kvazaar and x265 HEVC encoders on embedded system Nvidia Jetson platform', J. Real-Time Image Processing 2024, https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11554-024-01429-5); x265 versions, presets and CPU models were not seen. All comparisons are all-intra (intra-only) encoding, not general inter coding, and speed is compared at preset pairs matched for coding efficiency, so the two encoders run different presets (different work); the 2015-2016 numbers are against x265 of that era. The Kvazaar README itself carries no benchmark numbers. Counter-evidence: issue #378 (open since 2023-12-14, no maintainer reply) reports Kvazaar encoding slower than x265 in the reporter's test, 'not conforming to the paper'.
